attribution: by position inside a block: the harness sends the frozen scenario set in a fixed order and waits between each, so the n-th turn of a block is the n-th scenario. Blocks whose turn count does not match are reported as unattributed instead of being correlated by clock.
design: cold and warm arms alternated in ABBA order (cold,warm,warm,cold and the mirrored order); one process per cold block; identical scenario set and order in every block

environment_after.gpu: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 Laptop GPU, 900 MHz, 2100 MHz, 58, 17.28 W, 0x0000000000000020, 763 MiB, 6144 MiB

environment_before.gpu: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 Laptop GPU, 900 MHz, 2100 MHz, 59, 17.27 W, 0x0000000000000020, 721 MiB, 6144 MiB

readings: The first turn of a block is what a cold start actually costs a person: 4814.1 ms p50 cold (n=4, sd 119.7) against 3698.8 ms p50 warm (n=4, sd 264.3). Both arms are tight, so the roughly 1.1 s cold penalty is real and repeatable.

From the second turn onwards cold and warm are the same experience: 895.5 ms p50 cold against 852.8 ms warm. The whole-arm medians (930.3 vs 908.0 ms) hide the cold start entirely, which is why the first turn is reported apart.
Even a warm block pays 3.7 s on its own first turn, so what the first turn costs is not only model load: it is the first turn after a pause.

Transport and painting are not the cost. keystroke to submit 0.855 ms, bridge crossing 0.070 ms, queue wait 0.643 ms, publish to DOM 18.0 ms and DOM to paint 19.5 ms: about 39 ms of the roughly 926 ms a turn takes.

decision_ms has a p50 of 21.9 ms over 40 turns, which is the deterministic recognition doing its job, but a max of 15119.9 ms: a single model turn policy decision can still cost fifteen seconds, and that outlier is what drives the 15151.4 ms worst case of the whole run.
arguments_grounding_ms sits at 0.848 ms p50 (n=16), which is the promoted deterministic scope: this was the arm that used to cost about 1.0 s.
honesty: paint.observed is a post-mutation double-rAF proxy inside WebView2, not a confirmation from the OS compositor. It bounds when the DOM change was handed to the renderer; it does not prove the pixels reached the panel.
